title: Booking a private chef for your holiday cottage: the planning checklist
summary: Planning a private chef dinner in a holiday cottage? Check permissions, kitchen facilities, arrival times and dining space before booking.
body_markdown:
A big holiday house is built for time together. Too often, though, one person spends the afternoon in a supermarket queue and the evening at the hob while everyone else is at the table.


A private chef fixes that, and it’s one of the most popular ways to book us.


> “What I’ve loved is how hiring a private chef becomes the highlight of their holiday. Having someone create a personalized meal just for you really makes it special.”
> —[Chef Caitlin, private chef in Cornwall](https://yhangry.com/private-dining-cornwall-caitlin-yhangry/)


Looking at yhangry bookings in holiday cottages, lodges, barns and Airbnbs, more than four in ten are birthday celebrations and almost one in five is a hen or stag weekend. Nearly three-quarters take place on a Friday or Saturday night, usually the big night of the trip. It isn’t only a summer thing either: May and November are our busiest months for holiday-home dinners.


> “Cornwall is not just a summer spot. I’ve been busy even in January, February, and March.”
> — Chef Caitlin


Most of the planning comes down to making sure the house and the meal suit each other. Our data shows where people get caught out: holiday-home bookers are around eight times more likely than other customers to ask about equipment and crockery, and seven times more likely to raise access or arrival times. Here’s how to sort both before you travel.


### 1. Ask the property owner first


Before you request menus, check the house rules and tell the owner or agency what you’re planning. Ask about:


A dinner for the people already staying is often treated differently from a party with extra guests, so be clear which you’re planning. If the property has rules for outside suppliers, pass them to your chef before booking. A recommendation on a booking website doesn’t override the owner’s own rules.


### 2. Photograph the kitchen and dining space


Listing photos are taken to sell the house, not to show a chef what they’re working with. Ask the owner for current photos of:


This is the first thing most chefs ask for once a holiday-home booking is confirmed. Holiday lets vary a lot, but experienced chefs are used to working with them.


> “Airbnbs usually have the minimum available… Most of my events are in Airbnbs, so I’m sure we can make it work!”
> — Chef Marina


A quick description or a few photos of the kitchen helps them plan. If you don’t have photos yet, just send the property’s name or listing link. Many chefs will look it up themselves and check the kitchen from the listing.


Agas deserve a special mention, because they’re common in country cottages and they cook very differently from a standard oven.


> “We are able to use AGA ovens, however not all of our menus are suited to this appliance. Please let us know as early as possible if the only oven/hob available is an AGA.”
> — Chef Molly, Leeds


Small or under-equipped kitchens are the issue chefs raise most often after holiday-home bookings. One chef described a cottage kitchen so tight that the dining table encroached on the cooking area. Another spotted from the listing photos that a kitchen had almost no worktop space, and flagged it weeks ahead so the menu could be adapted. Telling your chef early means problems are solved before the night, not during it.


> “I have cooked delicious meals in very basic kitchens!”
> — Chef Sophie, Hove


A house that sleeps twelve won’t always have twelve matching plates either. Ask your chef whether you’ll need serving platters, extra cutlery or hired items. A quarter of holiday-home bookers ask exactly this, so you’re in good company.


### 3. Plan around your arrival


Many groups book the chef for the night they arrive, and that’s where timings get tight. One hen party could only get into their cottage from 5pm but had dinner booked for 8pm, so they checked with the chef that this left enough prep time.


Choose **one person** as the contact for both the property and the booking, and give them the full address, access instructions and arrival time. Holiday lets sometimes don’t have a house number until shortly before the stay, so send it to the chef as soon as you have it. Rural cottages often have patchy signal, so share a backup contact in advance, such as the house Wi-Fi or a landline.


### 4. Choose food that suits the stay


> “Some guests want a really upscale feel; others want it super casual. But overall, the vibe here is relaxed, delicious, and a little bit special.”
> — Chef Caitlin


Think about how the evening will actually go:


If the kitchen is limited, ask the chef what’s feasible before promising your group a particular format. Any extra equipment or staff should be agreed and included in the quote.


### 5. Agree how the house is left


A great dinner shouldn’t turn into a checkout problem. Confirm with your chef:


The good news: holiday-home dinners score as highly as any booking on yhangry, averaging 4.9 out of 5 for food. Reviews often mention chefs leaving the kitchen “cleaner than they found it”.

It often costs less than people expect, too.


> “People are often surprised — they assume hiring a private chef is a huge expense, but it often works out the same (or even less!) than dining out, especially when you factor in things like being able to bring your own drinks, staying in your comfy space, and having a completely bespoke menu.”

When you enquire, include the full property address, your date, the number of guests and your kitchen photos. Whether you’re in a Cotswolds barn, a Cornish cottage or a Lake District lodge, everyone gets to sit down together, including whoever usually does the cooking.


FAQs


Can I hire a private chef to cook in a holiday cottage or Airbnb?


Yes. Holiday cottages, lodges, barns and Airbnbs are some of the most popular places to book a yhangry chef. Check with the property owner first that outside chefs are allowed, and pass on any rules they have for suppliers.


What kitchen equipment does a private chef need?


Most chefs need a working oven, a hob and a clear sink and worktop area. Many bring their own pots, pans and utensils. Send photos of the kitchen when you enquire so the chef can plan the menu and bring whatever’s missing.


Can a private chef cook with an Aga?


Many can, but not every menu suits one. Tell your chef as early as possible if the only oven or hob in the property is an Aga.


What if the holiday let doesn’t have enough plates or cutlery?


Ask your chef. Some bring their own serving dishes, and others can arrange hire for an extra cost. Agree it in advance so it’s included in your quote.


Can the chef cook on the day we arrive?


Yes, but check the property’s check-in time first. The chef can’t start while the house is being cleaned between guests. If check-in is late, booking for your second night is often easier.


How much does a private chef cost for a holiday cottage?


It depends on the menu, group size and location. Many guests find it works out the same as eating out, or less, especially once you factor in bringing your own drinks. *\[Optional: “Holiday-home bookings on yhangry average around £80 per head.”\]*
